In summary, our research is concerned with
the nutritional content of commercially available foods for cats.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the majority of cat foods have high phosphorus and low calcium to phosphorus ratios, which are associated with renal disease.
the P content in the cat foods tested was higher than the recommended levels, and the Ca content was lower than the recommended levels.
the majority of cat foods are formulated to meet AAFCO requirements, but a significant number of foods exceed AAFCO guidelines for P content and Ca/P ratio.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no such thing as a “low phosphorus” cat food, and that all foods contain more phosphorus than is necessary for the cat.
there are a lot of cat foods with high P, low Ca, and high Ca:P.
there is a need to establish a maximum P level in cat foods.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current regulatory framework is inadequate to prevent the marketing of foods with excessive P and low Ca.
the P concentration in cat foods can be very high and that there are no established guidelines to help consumers make better choices.

pet food manufacturers should not be allowed to declare the P and Ca content on pet food labels without first having the values verified by an independent laboratory, which is a standard practice in the human food industry.
